state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's focus on the misconception that changing all values by the same proportion doesn't affect the range. Think about how altering the heights of the plants by the same amount might impact the range. What do you notice about the range when each plant grows by 3 cm?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Hmm, so if each plant grows by 3 cm, then like... the tallest one is still the tallest and the shortest is still the shortest, right? So I guess the difference between them would stay the same? But I'm confused because I thought adding the same amount to everything wouldn't change the range, so why would Katie be right?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think about how adding the same amount to each plant affects the overall spread of the heights. Consider the underlying misconception that changing all values by the same proportion doesn't impact the range. Can you see a connection between these ideas and why Katie might be correct in this scenario?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher repeatedly mentions the misconception but doesn't clarify the crucial distinction between proportional changes (multiplication) versus additive changes, leaving the student confused about why Katie is right when their intuition (which is actually correct) says the range stays the same with addition.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher fails to break the problem into manageable steps or scaffold appropriately; instead of helping the student work through calculations when they're confused, the teacher repeatedly references an abstract 'misconception about proportions' that isn't relevant to the student's actual error and doesn't adjust support when the student explicitly states confusion.
